Draw a triangle on a ball with three right angles.

Goal: I can describe how triangles on a sphere break Euclid's angle sum. (Enrichment, non-Euclidean.)

slides.title: The big idea
slides.html:
On a sphere, the "straight lines" are great circles, circles whose center is the sphere's center, like the equator and the lines of longitude. They give the shortest path between two points along the surface.

A triangle on a sphere can have three right angles: start at the North Pole, go down a longitude line to the equator, a quarter of the way around the equator, and back up. Its angle sum is 270 degrees. On a sphere every triangle's angles add to more than 180 degrees, and any two great circles meet, so there are no parallel lines. Enrichment: a non-Euclidean geometry.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.html: Why doesn't the 180 degree angle sum hold on a sphere?
slides.reveal: Its proof needs the Parallel Postulate, and on a sphere there are no parallel great circles.
